result:
Consider the lichen—that gray-green crust clinging to boulders, fence posts, the shoulders of old trees. It is easy to overlook, easy to mistake for dirt or decay. But lichen is not one organism at all; it is a partnership, a fungus and an alga (or sometimes a bacterium) living so intimately together that they become a single, nameable thing. Neither could survive alone on bare rock. Together, they can colonize stone that has never known soil.

Lichen teaches patience on a scale we can barely imagine. Some colonies grow less than a millimeter per year. A patch on an Arctic boulder may be older than the pyramids, older than agriculture itself—a slow green-gray thought accumulating across millennia. Scientists date glacier retreat by measuring how far lichen has spread: the longer the ice has been gone, the larger the colony. They are living clocks.

There's something quietly radical about this. We live in an age obsessed with speed—instant messages, same-day delivery, feeds refreshed by the second. And yet here is an organism that succeeds precisely by refusing hurry. It doesn't compete for light like a tree or flee predators like a deer. It simply persists, tolerating drought, cold, radiation, even the vacuum of space in some experiments.

Maybe that's the lesson hiding in plain sight on every weathered wall: survival isn't always about being fastest or strongest. Sometimes it's about finding your partner, settling onto hard ground, and growing—one imperceptible fraction of a millimeter at a time.
